Good at high T; fails for light atoms (Be, C, diamond) at low T

questions.question: Q1. Define linear expansivity α and write the formula.
questions.answer: α is the fractional increase in length per unit rise in temperature: α = ΔL/(L₀ΔT). So L = L₀(1+αΔT).

questions.question: Q2. Relate cubic, superficial and linear expansion coefficients.
questions.answer: For isotropic solids, superficial β = 2α and cubic γ = 3α. Thus a solid's volume change per degree is three times its linear change.
questions.example: A cube: each edge grows with α, volume with 3α.

questions.question: Q3. An iron rail of length 1.5 m, α = 11×10⁻⁶/°C, is heated by 50 °C. Find its increase in length.
questions.example: ≈ 0.8 mm; gaps left in rails to avoid buckling.

questions.question: Q4. Explain why gaps are left between railway joints and in bridges.
questions.answer: With temperature the rails expand; without gaps they would buckle or stress the structure. The gap absorbs the thermal expansion ΔL = αLΔT, preventing damage.
questions.shortcut: Gap absorbs ΔL = αLΔT; thermal stress avoidance.
questions.example: Expansion joints on bridges open with heat.

questions.question: Q5. A glass cube (α = 9×10⁻⁶/°C) of side 2 cm is heated by 40 °C. Find change in volume.
questions.answer: ΔV = γVΔT = 3αVΔT = 3×9×10⁻⁶×(2³)×40 = 3×9×10⁻⁶×8×40 = 8.64×10⁻³ cm³. ▥ 10.1–10.2 Linear, Superficial & Cubic Expansion  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Linear vs Superficial vs Cubic Expansion ▣ 10.3 Liquid Expansion & 10.4 Dulong-Petit

questions.question: Q6. Define absolute and apparent expansion of a liquid.
questions.answer: Absolute expansion = the true volume change of the liquid. Apparent expansion = what is observed, which is the liquid's expansion minus the container's expansion (the container also expands, so the liquid appears to rise less).
questions.example: The same liquid in a larger vessel shows less rise.

questions.question: Q7. A glass vessel (cubic γ_v=27×10⁻⁶/°C) holds mercury. Mercury's absolute γ=180×10⁻⁶/°C. Find apparent expansion.
Q8. Explain the anomalous (reverse) expansion of water between 0 °C and 4 °C.
questions.answer: Water contracts as it cools from 4 °C to 0 °C, so it is densest at 4 °C. This is anomalous and is why ice floats: the top layer can freeze while water below stays at 4 °C, protecting life in lakes.
questions.shortcut: Water densest at 4 °C; ice (0 °C) less dense → floats.
questions.example: Lakes freeze top-down because of this anomaly.

questions.question: Q9. State Dulong and Petit's law.
questions.answer: The molar specific heat of most crystalline solids at (moderately high) temperature is approximately constant: C_m ≈ 3R ≈ 25 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, independent of the element.
questions.example: A metal's heat capacity per mole is ~ 25 J/K.

questions.question: Q10. Two solid bars, α₁, α₂ and equal lengths. The coefficient of the composite? State how to find it.
questions.answer: For a composite bar in series, use the total change: L(α₁LΔT+α₂LΔT) = L(α₁+α₂)ΔT. A single effective α (equal-length halves) would be (α₁+α₂)/2; in general use series/parallel combination of the individual ΔL. ▥ 10.3 Liquid Expansion & 10.4 Dulong-Petit  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Apparent vs Real Expansion of Liquids Dulong–Petit: What It Says PROFESSOR'S THEORY & VIVA BANK   — the kinds of theory a professor / examiner actually asks
questions.shortcut: Sum ΔL of each part; equal halves → α_eff = (α₁+α₂)/2.
questions.example: Invar + steel reduces the overall expansion.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T1. Derive that γ = 3α for a solid.
theoryItems.answer: A cube of side L₀ expands to L₀(1+αΔT). Volume V = L³ ≈ L₀³[1+3αΔT] (ignoring higher terms). Since V = V₀(1+γΔT), comparing gives γ = 3α.
theoryItems.example: A rod, a plate and a block of the same solid expand consistently.

theoryItems.question: [State] T2. Define linear, superficial and cubical expansivity.
theoryItems.answer: Linear α = fractional increase in length per °C (L = L₀(1+αΔT)). Superficial β = 2α (area). Cubical γ = 3α (volume). For isotropic solids β = 2α, γ = 3α.
theoryItems.shortcut: α: length; β=2α: area; γ=3α: volume.

theoryItems.question: [Compare] T3. Compare the expansion of solids and liquids.
theoryItems.answer: Solids expand in all three dimensions (α, β, γ) and stay rigid. Liquids expand only in volume (no fixed shape) and show apparent expansion depending on the container. Solids have well-defined α; liquids have only γ.
theoryItems.shortcut: Solids: 3-D rigid; Liquids: volume only, container-dependent.
theoryItems.example: A solid bar stretches; a liquid just increases its level.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T4. Explain the measurement of linear expansion using a brass bar and a micrometer.
theoryItems.answer: The bar of known length L₀ at temperature θ₁ is clamped at one end; the free end, on heating to θ₂, pushes a lever/micrometer. Measuring the micrometer reading change ΔL gives α = ΔL/(L₀ΔT). α = measured extension / (L₀·ΔT).
theoryItems.shortcut: α = ΔL/(L₀ΔT) with a lever gauge.
theoryItems.example: Gives α of a metal; used for expansion coefficients.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T5. Explain absolute and apparent expansion of a liquid and their relation.
theoryItems.answer: Absolute expansion = the true change in liquid volume. Apparent = the observed change, which is the liquid's absolute expansion minus the container's expansion (the vessel also expands). Hence γ_app = γ_abs − γ_vessel.
theoryItems.example: The same liquid shows less rise in a larger vessel.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T6. Explain Dulong and Petit's law and its use.
theoryItems.answer: The molar specific heat of most crystalline solids is nearly constant, C_m ≈ 3R ≈ 25 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, independent of the element (at moderately high T). It lets one find an element's atomic mass from its specific heat: atomic mass × specific heat ≈ 25.
theoryItems.example: A low specific heat implies a high atomic mass.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T7. Explain the anomalous expansion of water between 0 °C and 4 °C and its consequences.
theoryItems.answer: Water contracts as it cools from 4 °C to 0 °C, so it is densest at 4 °C. This is why lakes freeze from the top down, ice floats, and aquatic life survives in winter.
theoryItems.shortcut: Densest at 4 °C; ice (0 °C) is less dense.
theoryItems.example: A thermometric scale for water must account for this anomaly.

theoryItems.question: [Why] T8. Why do bi-metal strips bend on heating, and how is this used?
theoryItems.answer: The two metals have different α; on heating, the metal with larger α expands more and goes to the outer side, bending the strip. This is used in thermostats and fire alarms: at a preset temperature the strip bends enough to close an electrical contact.
theoryItems.example: A thermostat switches heating off at the set temperature.

theoryItems.question: [Numerical] T9. A brass ring (α = 19×10⁻⁶/°C, D = 10 cm at 20 °C) must fit a 10.10 cm steel rod. Find the temperature to heat the ring.
theoryItems.example: ≈ 546 °C to slip the ring over the rod.

▣ 10.1–10.2 Linear, Superficial & Cubic Expansion
Q1. Define linear expansivity α and write the formula.
Answer:  α is the fractional increase in length per unit rise in temperature: α = ΔL/(L₀ΔT). So L = L₀(1+αΔT).
⚡ Shortcut:  L = L₀(1+αΔT).
Example:  α ≈ 12×10⁻⁶ /°C for iron.
Q2. Relate cubic, superficial and linear expansion coefficients.
Answer:  For isotropic solids, superficial β = 2α and cubic γ = 3α. Thus a solid's volume change per degree is three times its linear change.
⚡ Shortcut:  β = 2α, γ = 3α.
Example:  A cube: each edge grows with α, volume with 3α.
Q3. An iron rail of length 1.5 m, α = 11×10⁻⁶/°C, is heated by 50 °C. Find its increase in length.
⚡ Shortcut:  ΔL = αLΔT.
Example:  ≈ 0.8 mm; gaps left in rails to avoid buckling.
Q4. Explain why gaps are left between railway joints and in bridges.
Answer:  With temperature the rails expand; without gaps they would buckle or stress the structure. The gap absorbs the thermal expansion ΔL = αLΔT, preventing damage.
⚡ Shortcut:  Gap absorbs ΔL = αLΔT; thermal stress avoidance.
Example:  Expansion joints on bridges open with heat.
Q5. A glass cube (α = 9×10⁻⁶/°C) of side 2 cm is heated by 40 °C. Find change in volume.
⚡ Shortcut:  Use γ = 3α for volume change.
Example:  ≈ 8.6×10⁻³ cm³ expansion.

Q6. Define absolute and apparent expansion of a liquid.

Answer:  Absolute expansion = the true volume change of the liquid. Apparent expansion = what is observed, which is the liquid's expansion minus the container's expansion (the container also expands, so the liquid appears to rise less).
⚡ Shortcut:  γ_app = γ_abs − γ_vessel.
Example:  The same liquid in a larger vessel shows less rise.
Q7. A glass vessel (cubic γ_v=27×10⁻⁶/°C) holds mercury. Mercury's absolute γ=180×10⁻⁶/°C. Find apparent expansion.
⚡ Shortcut:  γ_app = γ_abs − γ_v.
Example:  ≈ 1.53×10⁻⁴ /°C.
Q8. Explain the anomalous (reverse) expansion of water between 0 °C and 4 °C.

Answer:  Water contracts as it cools from 4 °C to 0 °C, so it is densest at 4 °C. This is anomalous and is why ice floats: the top layer can freeze while water below stays at 4 °C, protecting life in lakes.
⚡ Shortcut:  Water densest at 4 °C; ice (0 °C) less dense → floats.
Example:  Lakes freeze top-down because of this anomaly.
Q9. State Dulong and Petit's law.
Answer:  The molar specific heat of most crystalline solids at (moderately high) temperature is approximately constant: C_m ≈ 3R ≈ 25 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, independent of the element.
⚡ Shortcut:  Molar C_v of solids ≈ 3R ≈ 25 J/mol·K.
Example:  A metal's heat capacity per mole is ~ 25 J/K.
Q10. Two solid bars, α₁, α₂ and equal lengths. The coefficient of the composite? State how to find it.

Answer:  For a composite bar in series, use the total change: L(α₁LΔT+α₂LΔT) = L(α₁+α₂)ΔT. A single effective α (equal-length halves) would be (α₁+α₂)/2; in general use series/parallel combination of the individual ΔL.
⚡ Shortcut:  Sum ΔL of each part; equal halves → α_eff = (α₁+α₂)/2.
Example:  Invar + steel reduces the overall expansion.
